newsitem.title: ITALY: Parity is hot potato as lira's ERM bid draws near.
newsitem.headline: Parity is hot potato as lira's ERM bid draws near.

text.p: Italy is hardening its resolve to return the vagabond lira to Europe's exchange rate mechanism after four years out in the cold, with an application to rejoin the currency grid looking inevitable by the end of November.
Market watchers are assessing at what rate against the mark the lira can be reinstated and politicians, industrialists and economists are pitching into the politically charged debate.
Italian Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco is the latest to join the chorus, telling a meeting late on Thursday that Italy expected to put the lira in the ERM by the end of November.

"I think a balanced solution with the mark between 1,000 and 1,050 lire would be more than reasonable, especially as we are in a situation in which we still have a little potential competitive advantage," Visco said.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said this week Italy would probably ask for re-entry to the ERM during a weekend at the end of November, once the 1997 draft budget passes through the lower house of parliament where it is now under scrutiny.
Ciampi, a former Italian prime minister and central bank governor, cited a possible rate "slightly above 1,000 per mark."

Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, another former Italian premier and central banker, said it would be hard for Italy or other nations to impose a rate out of line with the level the lira has held for months on foreign exchange markets.
But Italian industry wants a weaker level of 1,050, with Giorgio Fossa, chairman of employers' association Confindustria, saying this was compatible with Italy's high interest rates.

The lira's parity within the ERM is a bone of contention with Italy's EU partners. French industrialists complain they have been hit by the competitive edge enjoyed by Italian producers as a result of heavy devaluation.

Shortly before it left the ERM in September 1992 the lira had a central rate of 802.49 per mark and 239.27 per French franc but by early 1995 it had plummeted to a historic low of 1,275 per mark, a devalution of more than 50 percent, and to 359.80 per franc. It is now around 298.00 against the franc.

Since 1995 the lira has risen with Italy's political fortunes, staying between 990 and 1,010 per mark since September. Foreign exchange dealers suspect the steadying hand of the Bank of Italy has intervened to prevent further appreciation.

In order to return to the ERM, Italy must ask for a meeting of the EU's monetary committee of senior finance ministry and central bank officials, which would have to agree whether and at what central rate the currency could join.

But an EU official in Brussels signalled on Friday that the decision was likely to require Finance Ministers' involvement, saying: "We won't have to spend too long at civil service level because this is so politically charged."

Economists say based on the performance of the lira in the past six months, a rate of 1,010-1,020 would be reasonable. Marcello Pericoli, economist at San Paolo bank in London, saw Italy asking for 1,025, slightly weaker than today's level as Italian interest rates were expected to fall by the year end.
But several analysts point out that, given the political stakes, a level of around 1,000 may be more likely.
Stephen King, chief European economist at HSBC Markets, said a trade off was needed between Italy's ideal of 1,050 and France's preference for something closer to 950.

"A thousand would seem to be a reasonable compromise and given we've been trading at approximately 1,000 for the last three or four months it does look as though that's the kind of implicit target the Italians are aiming for," King said.
